consensus_summary: The consensus holds that 'coin' has no single settled biblical symbolism; its meaning is context-dependent. The most prominent reading is the tribute-coin logic of image and ownership: the coin bears Caesar's image and belongs to Caesar, while humans bear God's image and belong to God. Well-recognized alternatives include the lost coin as the lost sinner sought by God (with a patristic extension in which the coin is the image of God in the soul), thirty pieces of silver as betrayal/blood money, the widow's mites as sacrificial giving, the vineyard denarius as grace, the temple-tax coin as providential provision, and money generally as mammon/stewardship.
book_summary: The book gives a single unified identification: the coin is a person as the owner's stamped image-bearer — refined like gold, bearing the sign, name, and image of God or of the beast, assigned a value, and sought when lost. The recovered coin pictures the repentant sinner, and human valuation is contrasted with God's valuation. It draws in census/ransom money (Ex 30), vow valuation of persons (Lev 27), the lost coin, the temple-tax coin, the tribute coin, the widow's mites, refining imagery (1 Pet 1:7), and the mark/name on foreheads (Rev 13-14), with patristic support (Tertullian, Gregory the Great, Gregory of Nyssa).
consensus_core_identification: Coin = context-dependent symbol, with the leading reading being image/ownership/allegiance (the coin bears its issuer's image and belongs to him; humans bear God's image and belong to God), alongside the lost coin as the lost sinner and other context-specific meanings.
book_core_identification: Coin = the human person as a stamped image-bearer belonging to and valued by an owner (God or the beast), refined, assigned worth, and sought when lost; the found coin = the repentant sinner.
boundary_disagreement: The book fuses two of the consensus's leading readings (image/ownership from the tribute coin; the lost coin as the sought sinner) into one governing identification — person as image-bearing coin — and treats it as the coin's meaning across contexts rather than one context-bound meaning among several. In doing so it reclassifies cases the consensus assigns other meanings: the widow's mites (consensus: sacrificial giving) and the temple-tax coin (consensus: providential provision) are folded into the person-as-valued-coin scheme, and it adds cases absent from the consensus (Ex 30 ransom money, Lev 27 valuation of persons, Rev 13-14 mark/name on foreheads, 1 Pet 1:7 refining). It also drops or de-centers consensus meanings such as thirty pieces of silver as betrayal and money as mammon.
rationale: The book's central referent is recognizably the consensus's most theologically developed reading: the human being as God's coinage, stamped with His image and belonging to Him, precious and sought when lost. Response A's primary meaning plus its lost-coin alternative, and Response C's minority 'humanity bearing the divine image' alternative, cover this core almost exactly, and the book's own patristic citations (Tertullian, Gregory the Great) are the very authorities the consensus names. So this is not NOVEL and not DIVERGENT. However, the book materially changes the boundary: where the consensus insists the coin is polyvalent and context-controlled, the book universalizes the image-bearer reading, extends it via Revelation's mark of the beast (allowing the coin-person to bear either God's or the beast's image — an extension no consensus response contains) and via person-valuation texts, and reclassifies passages (widow's mites, temple tax) that the consensus reads otherwise. That is real boundary disagreement within a preserved central referent: REFINED.
strongest_objection: One could argue for MATCH, since the book's core (person as God's image-bearing coin, sought when lost) is essentially Response A's primary meaning combined with its first alternative, and the patristic sources coincide; on that view the extra material (refining, mark of the beast, valuation texts) is elaboration rather than a changed extension. Against this, the book's unification of the symbol across contexts, its two-owner scheme (God or the beast), and its reclassification of the widow's mites and temple-tax coin go beyond mere wording and constitute a genuine boundary shift, and the printed citations (e.g., Rev 13:16; 14:1, which mention no coin) only partially establish the unified claim.
